proof:
# Cap variance products with zero phases in arbitrary dimension

Let a proper section of a d-simplex have raw barycentric coefficients c_i, actual section centroid b, and cap fraction F. The inequality

    F(1-F)<=d^d product_(i!=j)b_i for every j        (1)

holds in either of these two regimes:

* one strict sign is represented by exactly one raw coefficient, with arbitrarily many coefficients of the other sign and arbitrarily many zero coefficients;
* each strict sign is represented by at most two raw coefficients, with arbitrarily many zero coefficients.

In particular (1) holds whenever at most four raw coefficients are nonzero, in every ambient simplex dimension. This is a boundary/low-phase theorem, not a proof for unrestricted raw coefficients in arbitrary dimension.

## 1. Independence of the zero phases

Use independent unit-rate exponentials Y_i and condition on sum c_iY_i=0. As proved in `candidate c324e86ba3893a31`, their conditional means are mu_i=d b_i. Every zero-coefficient Y_i is still independent unit-rate exponential under this conditioning and has mu_i=1. The cap probability F depends only on the nonzero phases.

If j is a nonzero phase, the product in (1) is therefore the product of the conditional means of the OTHER nonzero phases. If j is a zero phase, it is the product of the means of ALL nonzero phases. Thus an omitted zero coefficient requires the latter, stronger-looking active-phase product; it does not follow merely by citing an excluded-coordinate theorem in the smaller dimension.

## 2. One coefficient against all the others

By reversal take the sole positive coefficient to be p>0 and the strict negatives to be -q_i, i=1,...,m. Put eta_i=p/(p+q_i) in (0,1). Direct elimination of the sole positive exponential gives

    F=product eta_i,
    mu_i=eta_i for the negative phases,
    mu_positive=sum_i(1-eta_i).

The conditional law of the negative exponentials is a product with means eta_i, and the last identity also follows from the zero linear constraint. If j is the positive phase, the excluded product is F>=F(1-F). If j is a negative phase, it is

    F sum_i(1-eta_i)/eta_j>=F(1-F),

because eta_j<=1 and 1-product eta_i<=sum_i(1-eta_i). If j is a zero phase, the product of all nonzero means is

    F sum_i(1-eta_i)>=F(1-F).

This proves (1) in the first regime, including m=1. The elementary product inequality follows by telescoping 1-product eta_i into sum_i (1-eta_i)product_(k<i)eta_k.

## 3. Two positive and two negative phases

Let the four nonzero coefficients be (p,q,-r,-s), all magnitudes positive. Their conditional means are mu_i=3b_i^*, where b^* is the actual section centroid in the associated tetrahedron. If the omitted index j is active, the strict inequality follows from the complete tetrahedral theorem in `candidate fa0b1651cc72d020`.

For an omitted zero phase, the needed claim is

    product_(i=0)^3 mu_i>F(1-F).                  (2)

Here is a complete additional positive-polynomial certificate. Set

    D=pq(r+s)+rs(p+q),
    E=(p+r)^2(p+s)^2(q+r)^2(q+s)^2 D^4.

For a>=b define M_ab(u,v)=u^a v^b+u^b v^a when a>b, and M_aa(u,v)=u^a v^a. For ordered pairs ab>=cd in lexicographic order, define

    S_(ab,cd)=M_ab(p,q)M_cd(r,s)+M_cd(p,q)M_ab(r,s)

when ab!=cd, and S_(ab,ab)=M_ab(p,q)M_ab(r,s). Then the exact identity is

    product_i mu_i-F(1-F)=(sum C_(ab,cd) S_(ab,cd))/E, (3)

with this full coefficient table, all other coefficients zero:

    77,60: 1       77,51: 4       77,42: 7       77,33: 9
    76,61: 5       76,52: 17      76,43: 28
    75,62: 10      75,53: 29      75,44: 40
    74,63: 10      74,54: 24
    73,64: 5       73,55: 9
    72,65: 1
    66,62: 24      66,53: 76      66,44: 104
    65,63: 53      65,54: 134
    64,64: 68      64,55: 118
    55,55: 210.

To verify (3), substitute the actual centroid formulas (2) and cap fraction (3) from the tetrahedral cap-variance source, with mu_i=3b_i^*, clear E, and collect symmetric pairs. This gives precisely the displayed 23 entries, or 129 positive monomials after expansion. All terms and the denominator are strictly positive. Thus (2) follows without any restriction on repeated magnitudes or on the original ambient dimension.

The first regime covers the other sign partitions with at most four nonzero coefficients. Section 1 then proves every omitted-index case in (1). No limiting statement is needed to add zero coefficients: their conditional independence is exact.
